blocks.prompt: Slow on Purpose
blocks.text:
A sloth spends almost its whole life hanging upside down in a tree. Its claws curve like hooks and lock around a branch, so hanging takes it almost no effort. A sloth can sleep, eat, and even have a baby without letting go.

Why is a sloth so slow? The answer is in its food. A sloth eats leaves, and leaves are a poor meal. They are tough, and they carry very little energy. A sloth's stomach works so slowly that one leaf can take a month to digest. With so little fuel coming in, the sloth cannot afford to rush. It travels about forty yards in a day. A person can walk that far in half a minute.

Slowness also keeps the sloth alive. Harpy eagles and jaguars hunt by spotting movement. A sloth that barely moves is hard to notice, and the algae growing in its fur turns it faintly green, exactly the color of the leaves around it. The sloth is not being lazy. It is hiding in plain sight, and it is doing it on purpose.

blocks.prompt: The Weekly Climb Down
blocks.text:
A sloth is built around a single problem: leaves are barely worth eating. They are tough, hard to break down, and packed with almost no energy. A sloth solves this by spending as little as possible. It has about a third less muscle than other mammals its size. It lets its body temperature drift up and down with the day instead of burning fuel to stay warm. It moves roughly forty yards in twenty-four hours. Nearly everything about a sloth is a way of not spending energy it does not have.

The design has some strange bonuses. Most mammals, from mice to giraffes, have exactly seven bones in the neck. Three-toed sloths can have up to nine, which lets them swivel their heads almost all the way around without moving the rest of the body. Sloths are also surprisingly good swimmers. In water they move about three times faster than on land, and they can slow their heart rate and stay under for up to forty minutes.

Then there is the part that makes no sense. Once a week or so, a sloth climbs all the way down its tree to go to the bathroom on the forest floor. On the ground it is slow, clumsy, and defenseless. More than half of all sloth deaths happen during this trip. An animal this careful with its energy and its safety takes a serious risk every week, and scientists are still arguing about why.

blocks.prompt: The Cost of Being Slow
blocks.text:
Nothing about a sloth is an accident. Every part of it answers the same question: how do you survive on a food nobody else wants?

Sloths eat leaves. Leaves are abundant, which is the good news, and nearly worthless, which is the rest of it. They are low in energy and defended with tough fibers and mild toxins. A sloth's answer is a large, multi-chambered stomach that ferments leaves for weeks. A single meal can take a month to pass through. A full stomach can make up nearly a third of a sloth's body weight, which means a sloth is often carrying more dinner than muscle.

Everything else follows from that budget. A sloth's metabolic rate is among the lowest of any mammal. It carries about a third less muscle than a mammal of its size should. It does not shiver, and it lets its body temperature rise and fall with the forest air. Its claws hook over a branch and hold by tendon rather than by effort, so hanging costs it almost nothing, awake or asleep. It travels around forty yards a day. Slowness is not the sloth's weakness. It is the whole design, and it works: harpy eagles and jaguars hunt by detecting motion, and a sloth supplies almost none.

The fur takes the strategy further. Sloth hair is grooved and holds water, and green algae grow inside those grooves, tinting the animal the exact color of its background. Living in that fur is a small community of moths and beetles found almost nowhere else. Scientists think the moths and the algae and the sloth trade favors, though exactly which favors is still debated.

And yet the design has one hole in it. About once a week, a sloth climbs down, digs a small hole at the base of its tree, and goes to the bathroom on the ground. It is the most dangerous thing a sloth does. More than half of recorded sloth deaths occur on these trips. Why an animal so careful would take that risk, week after week, remains one of the better arguments in tropical biology. The moth hypothesis is one answer. Fertilizing its own tree is another. Nobody has settled it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Folivore: an animal that lives on leaves
Roughly 30 percent less muscle than expected for its size
Grooved hair farms its own algae
Cryptoses moths live only in sloth fur
Over half of recorded deaths occur on the weekly descent
Its extinct cousins, the ground sloths, grew elephant-sized

blocks.prompt: The Sloth's Argument for Being Slow
blocks.text:
There is an old joke that the sloth is nature's laziest animal. It is a bad joke, because laziness implies a choice, and the sloth has almost none. Every strange thing about it follows from one hard fact: its ancestors committed to a diet of leaves, and leaves do not pay well.

Leaves are a strange thing to build a body around. There are more of them than anything else in a rainforest, and almost nothing else wants them. That is the deal. A leaf is mostly cellulose, stiffened for structure and often laced with mild toxins, and it carries very little usable energy. To live on leaves you need a fermentation vat and a great deal of patience. The sloth has both. Its multi-chambered stomach holds microbes that break down fiber over weeks, and a single meal may take a month to complete the journey. A full digestive system can account for close to a third of the animal's weight. The sloth spends much of its life carrying its own dinner.

Once you accept that budget, the rest of the sloth stops looking absurd and starts looking like arithmetic. Its metabolic rate is among the lowest measured in any mammal. It carries roughly thirty percent less muscle than a mammal its size should, because muscle is expensive to keep. It cannot shiver, so it does not try, and instead lets its body temperature drift with the air around it. Its claws curve into hooks and lock over a branch by tendon rather than by effort, which means hanging costs it nearly nothing, awake or asleep. It covers about forty yards on an average day. None of this is laziness. It is a creature living within its means.

Slowness pays a second dividend that the joke misses entirely. The animals that eat sloths, harpy eagles and jaguars and ocelots, hunt largely by detecting movement. A sloth that barely moves barely registers. Its camouflage runs deeper still: sloth hair is grooved and holds moisture, and algae grow in those grooves until the animal is tinted the precise green of the canopy behind it. That fur also houses moths and beetles found almost nowhere else on Earth, a small private ecosystem riding through the trees.

So we have an animal optimized, with real elegance, for spending nothing and being noticed by no one. Which makes its one weekly habit almost impossible to explain. Roughly once a week, a sloth releases its branch and climbs all the way to the forest floor. It digs a shallow hole near the base of its tree, goes to the bathroom, covers the hole, and climbs back up. On the ground it is slow, badly built for walking, and visible to everything. More than half of recorded sloth deaths occur during this descent. An animal that has spent millions of years learning to be invisible steps into the open, on schedule, and pays for it.

Nobody has settled why. One idea is that the sloth is fertilizing its own tree. Another is that the trip serves the moths in its fur, which lay their eggs in the dung and later return to the sloth, carrying nutrients that feed the algae the sloth may be eating. A third is simply that the behavior is old, inherited, and no longer serves any purpose at all.

The sloth, in other words, is not a failure of ambition. It is a solution, and a good one, to a problem most animals refuse to take on. And like most good solutions, it still has one part nobody can quite account for.
